set.summary: An Israeli military-intelligence cell of Egyptian Jews planted incendiary devices at post offices, US information libraries and a British-owned cinema in Alexandria and Cairo. According to the Jewish Virtual Library account, Israel did not want British troops to leave the Canal Zone, and the operations were meant to show Egypt's new rulers as unreliable; the Israel Ministry of Defense Archives says the aim was to sabotage Egypt's relations with Western states. The network was caught; two members were hanged in early 1955 and others died in custody or were imprisoned. Defence Minister Pinhas Lavon resigned in February 1955; whether he gave the order became a political scandal that resurfaced in 1960-61.

add_cite.quote: The Israelis, meanwhile, did not want the British to leave.

add_cite.quote: make it clear to the whole world that Egypt’s new rulers were nothing but a group of foolhardy extremists, unreliable and unworthy of taking charge of an asset as important as the Suez Canal

set.summary: Yamit was a planned Israeli town in the Rafah salient of north-eastern Sinai, one of the settlements the government encouraged there after 1971; according to a member of its founding American garin, the group began building it on 17 January 1975. It became the largest of 14 Sinai settlements (about 600 houses by 1982).

set.summary: Three members of the Japanese Red Army, acting for the PFLP, opened fire in the arrivals hall at Lod Airport on 30 May 1972. Sources give 24 killed (Israel State Archives, count at the scene), 25 (a Cambridge University Press chapter) or 26 (later counts, e.g. ADST): 17 Puerto Rican Christian pilgrims, 8 Israelis including biophysicist Aharon Katzir, and a Canadian. Wounded figures range from 'over 70' (Israel State Archives) to 78 (a Cambridge chapter; a Puerto Rican memorial text). Two attackers died; Kozo Okamoto was captured.

'over 70' per Israel State Archives; 78 per Cambridge chapter and a Puerto Rican memorial text. Total killed: 24 (State Archives at the scene) to 26.
